report.source_text: In his early 50s, the patient was incidentally found to have proteinuria during a routine check by his general practitioner, despite never experiencing urinary tract symptoms. This led to an extended examination of the kidneys (see timeline below) due to differential diagnoses such as renal cancer, glomerulonephritis, diabetic kidney failure and myelomatosis. The patient’s renal function and proteinuria were regularly monitored at a nephrology department, and medication for hypertension (losartan) was attempted as a treatment to decrease the proteinuria.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A Caucasian male in his 70s with a monozygotic twin brother presented with a multisystemic clinical syndrome spanning decades. Since young age, he exhibited black spots on underpants and bed sheets (homogentisic acid in urine). In his early 40s, visible pigmentation appeared on the sclera, ears, and fingers. In his early 50s, he developed proteinuria (incidentally discovered despite no urinary symptoms) and progressive knee arthropathy. By his 50s-60s, he had developed tendinopathy, osteopenia, secondary glaucoma, mitral valve calcification, and black urinary and prostate stones. The diagnosis was triggered when his twin brother underwent surgery and surgeons intraoperatively encountered bone tissue with distinctive black discoloration, prompting procedure termination. This clinical finding prompted investigation of both brothers. The diagnosis was conclusively established through a diagnostic triad: (1) urine spot test for homogentisic acid (HGA) in both brothers, (2) intraoperative observation of black bone discoloration (ochronotic pigmentation) in the twin brother, and (3) genetic DNA testing of the twin brother revealing heterozygous pathogenic variants c.481G>A, p.(Gly161Arg) and c.1017G>T, p.(Met339Ile). The patient subsequently underwent total hip arthroplasty where distinctive black discoloration was observed on the femur head, further confirming ochronotic bone involvement. Spinal cysts were identified in the corpus of Th9 and Th10 on high-resolution CT imaging.
